title: On the Limits of Quantum Multiparty Simultaneous Communication
authors: Pedro Montealegre, Ivan Rapaport, Jorge Valenzuela
abstract: The Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model provides a fundamental framework for comparing classical and quantum communication. For two players, Gavinsky et al. (STOC 2006) established a separation underlying the incomparability of shared randomness and quantum communication: \textsc{Index Coordination} needs $O(\log n)$ public-coin bits but $Ω(n^{1/3})$ bounded-error qubits.   In this work, we establish a multiparty exponential separation through $\operatorname{IC}_{k,n}$, a natural $k$-party generalization of \textsc{Index Coordination}. Public-coin protocols solve it unambiguously with maximum message length $O(\log n)$ bits. In contrast, quantum SMP protocols without shared entanglement or public coins require maximum message length $Ω(n^{1-1/k})$ qubits in the unambiguous regime and $Ω(n^{(k-1)/(k+1)})$ qubits in the bounded-error regime. A classical private-coin protocol matches the unambiguous bound, so quantum communication provides no asymptotic advantage over private randomness in this regime. For fixed error parameters, all constants are independent of $k$, establishing the exponential separation for every integer-valued function $k=k(n)\ge2$, without restricting its growth. Both quantum lower bounds become $Ω(n)$ when $k\ge c\log n$ for any fixed $c>0$, matching the full-input protocol and yielding tight linear complexity in both regimes.   Our results demonstrate that quantum superposition cannot efficiently simulate the coordination afforded by public randomness, extending this separation to arbitrary $k$. To bound success probabilities for multiparty product states, we prove an exact factorization theorem for unambiguous quantum state identification, which may be of independent mathematical interest.
summary: This work analyzes the communication complexity of a multiparty coordination problem, showing that while public randomness offers a significant advantage, unentangled quantum communication does not surpass the power of classical private randomness in the bounded-error regime. The research establishes an exponential separation based on the number of players, providing deep insights into the role of shared randomness versus quantum superposition.
main_problem: The paper establishes an exponential separation between the communication power of classical shared randomness (public coins) and unentangled quantum communication in a multiparty setting.
main_result: It shows that for the generalized Index Coordination problem, quantum communication without shared entanglement offers no asymptotic advantage over classical private randomness in the bounded-error regime, while public randomness provides a significant advantage.
method: The authors employ techniques like the Parity Collapse method and information-pooling arguments, utilizing the Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean inequality to derive lower bounds on message size.
model_or_system: The study uses the Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model generalized to $k$ players, comparing the resources of classical private randomness, classical public randomness, and unentangled quantum superposition.
key_observables: Maximum message length required by the players, measured in bits (public coins) or qubits (quantum communication).
important_parameters: The number of players ($k$), the input size ($n$), and the error parameter ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The quantum protocols considered lack shared entanglement or public coins, and the results hold for fixed error parameters $\epsilon$.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the paper relies on summarizing bounds in a table (Table 1) comparing message lengths across different models.
paper_structure: The paper first generalizes the Index Coordination problem to $k$ parties. It then derives lower bounds for the unambiguous and bounded-error regimes using techniques like the RAC inequality and AM-GM inequality, culminating in the explicit separation results.
why_interesting: The findings provide fundamental limits on how quantum information can simulate classical coordination mechanisms, which has implications for quantum cryptography and distributed quantum computation protocols.
